C++ is a "high level" language. The CPU doesn't directly understand C++, it has to be converted into machine code. That's what the compiler does.

The PS2 and the Xbox use different machine code. They "speak different languages" in a sense. Some C++ compiled for the PS2 just won't make sense to an Xbox.

That's one reason. Another is that the hardware is just different. For example the PS2 game might have code that uses the PS2's special co-processors, but they just don't exist on Xbox. For some things they might have equivalent hardware (e.g. they both have GPUs, they both have controller ports, etc), but it just works differently so code written for one won't work on the other.

Then there's the OS. A modern PS4 and Xbox One are actually very similar on the hardware level. They have more or less the same CPU, which understands the same machine code, and most of the rest of the hardware is also very similar. But a PS4 game still won't work on an Xbox One. The Operating System (or System Software as its often called on consoles) provides a lot of features that games use. Using the hardware goes via the OS using an Application Programmer's Interface (API). The two consoles have different APIs for things like playing sounds or drawing graphics, so a game written for one won't work on the other.

Other people are saying the opposite because they've missed the fact that the option which loses on first preferences is eliminated, and at that point it's irrelevant how many people put it as their second choice.

The proposed deal would inevitably be eliminated. Then it will be a straight shoot between remain and no deal once the deal votes have been redistributed. The second choices for remain and no deal voters will never come into play.

Other counting methods could make the deal much more likely to win, such as approval or score voting. But that shows the inherent problem with multiple choice referendums, there isn't necessarily a clear answer for which deserves to win even once you've ask people which options they prefer.

One option is Condorcet voting. Voters would rank each option from 1 to 3 (or just a 1st and 2nd preference), and then the votes are counted as if it was 3 referendums, each pitting one option against another. If an option wins 2 of those votes, it wins overall.

The big problem is it's not guaranteed to produce a winner. It could come out as Option A winning over Option C, Option C winning over Option B, and Option B winning over Option A. So there would also need to be a fallback way of picking a winner if that happens.

More likely it would just be two questions. That's the most tried and tested way of running referendums with more than 2 outcomes. My problem with that is that it introduces the need for tactical voting, and that the order in which the questions are asked affects the result. Asking "Option X or Option Y?" then "If Option X, Option Z or Option W?" could end up with a different result to "Option Z or Option W?" then "If Option W, Option X or Option Y?".

With standard online multiplayer, not everything suffers from lag. For example, you can move the camera around without needing to wait for the server to respond, so it can be smooth and responsive even with a poor connection.

That won't be possible with a cloud gaming service. Your device isn't doing any of the game's movement logic, it's just receiving a video. So even for stuff like moving the camera, it will always lag behind your inputs by however many milliseconds it takes for your input data to get to the server and to receive video data in response.

There used to be many banks throughout the UK that issued "promissory notes". They were basically notes promising that the issuing bank is holding that many pounds on behalf of the owner of that note.

Then the central bank took over that role, and no new licenses to issue notes were given out. Over time all the licenses for commercial banks in England and Wales were cancelled, leaving the central bank as the sole body that issued notes.

But that didn't happen in Scotland and Northern Ireland. Banks in those nations kept their licenses. Partly because people liked having their own unique Scottish/Northern Irish notes and didn't want central bank ones.

The way these banks operate is that in their vaults they have central bank notes worth millions of pounds (e.g. a "titan" note is worth £100m), and all the notes they issue must be backed by these special central bank notes.

As for territories, it's just whatever makes sense for them. Some decided to have their own pounds pegged 1 to 1 with British pounds, others decided to use US Dollars presumably due to their proximity to the US.

The main reason you end up with a 2 party system is the First Past the Post voting system. That's where districts/constituencies are represented by a single person, and that person is whoever got more votes than anyone else.

That system naturally tends towards having 2 main parties. It's very difficult for smaller parties to gain anything because you need to be more popular than any other party in a single constituency to win anything. Even if you pick up a decent percentage of votes across the entire country, it means nothing if you aren't the most popular in any specific place. And that means voting for those parties is usually pointless because they have very little chance of winning anything.

To get away from a 2 party system you need to change the voting system. There are various proportional voting systems where your overall percentage of votes roughly translates into how many seats you get in parliament. That makes it easier for smaller parties because now votes for them aren't wasted, and can actually help them win something.

But how do you change the system? In a certain country, Parliament would need to pass a law to change it. But to pass a law, the majority of Parliament needs to support it, and the majority of Parliament is the party that won under FPTP. So they're not going to want to change to a system that will give other parties more power. Nor will most of their voters want it.

I don't know as much about another country, but as I understand it changing the voting system would need a constitutional amendment, and that's even harder to do.

There are some similarities to the relationship between the central government and subnational entities in the United States, but also big differences.

They are similar in the sense that there are some different laws in each subnational entity, but they all share the same citizenship, currency (although different banknotes), military, foreign relations, etc.

The big difference is that the United Kingdom is a unitary state, not a federation. In the US, states have a constitutional right to govern themselves to some degree. The federal government can't just suspend or get rid of a state government. But in the UK, any government within its borders exists at the will of the central Parliament.

Since the late 90s, 3 of the 4 constituent parts have their own governments. Then there's the largest part, which is ruled directly by the central Parliament. This largest part does have a lot of its own laws now, as a consequence of the fact the other parts have their own governments to handle those things.

Even before this there were significant differences between the parts. When two of the parts joined together, part of the deal was that one would keep its own legal system, which is significantly different to the other's. So even though they were ruled by the same Parliament for nearly 300 years, a lot of stuff was still different in one compared to the other. It was similar for another part, but less so for the third as that was considered part of the largest part for a few centuries. Even now the third shares the largest part's legal system, and the third's assembly has a bit less power than the governments of the other two devolved parts.

As for the name, "country" is generally preferred. "Constituent country" is used if you need to differentiate them from a country in the sense of a sovereign state. This is a big generalisation of course. But generally speaking different kinds of nationalism dominate.

A certain game came on a DVD, not a CD. So in both cases it's the same amount of storage.

A game like that is made up of lots of repeated data. There are loads of dungeons in it but if you look around the dungeons are mostly made up of the same models and textures repeated lots of times. So it doesn't need unique copies of that data for every single place it appears in the game (although it may be duplicated a few times for performance reasons).

You can't do that with video. Video is compressed in various ways, including only storing the changes from one frame to the next instead of the whole thing. So In a way it can also reuse data to some extent.

But if one episode of a show reuses a set from a previous episode there's no way to reuse the same bit of data for both episodes. We can easily tell it's the same scenery, but as far as the DVD player is concerned it's completely separate. It has no knowledge of what's in the scene, it's just looking at pixel values.
